title: Karl Marx

cards.h: The most-asked thinker in Paper I
cards.b:
Karl Marx (1818–1883) was born in Trier, Germany. He was a journalist and a revolutionary, and spent most of his life as an exile in London, where he studied in the British Museum.

Key works: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts (1844), The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels (1848), A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859) and Capital, volume one (1867).

PYQ analysis puts Marx at the top of the most-asked thinkers. You already met his theory of the state; this lesson covers the rest of his system.

Lenin said Marxism has three sources:

German philosophy

From Hegel, Marx took the dialectic: history moves through conflict. But he turned Hegel "right side up": matter and economics drive history, not ideas.

English political economy

From Adam Smith and David Ricardo, he took the labour theory of value.

French socialism

From Saint-Simon, Fourier and others, the vision of a society without exploitation.

In the 1859 Preface, Marx gives his theory of history in a few lines.

To live, people must produce. In producing, they enter relations of production that match the level of the forces of production (tools, skills, technology). Together these form the economic base. On it rises a legal and political superstructure.

"It is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but their social being that determines their consciousness."
Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859)

"The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles." So begins the Manifesto's first section.

Each mode of production has its own ruling and ruled class:

  • Primitive communism: no classes.
  • Ancient slavery: masters and slaves.
  • Feudalism: lords and serfs.
  • Capitalism: bourgeoisie and proletariat.
  • Communism: classes end.

When forces of production outgrow old relations, an era of social revolution begins.

In the 1844 Manuscripts, the young Marx says workers under capitalism are alienated, or estranged, in four ways:

  • From the product they make, which belongs to someone else.
  • From the act of labour, which feels forced, not free.
  • From their species-being, their human nature as free, creative producers.
  • From other people, who become rivals.

This idea made Marx important to humanist thinkers in the 20th century.

Marx asks: where does profit come from? His answer is surplus value.

The worker sells their labour power for a wage, which is the value needed to keep them alive. But in a working day they create more value than their wage. The extra goes to the capitalist as profit.

So exploitation is built into capitalism, even when the contract is "fair". This is the core argument of Capital.

Competition also pushes capitalists to replace workers with machines. Marx said this leads to a falling rate of profit and repeated crises.

Capitalism creates its own "gravediggers": the proletariat. As workers gather in factories, they develop class consciousness. Marx calls the move from a class "in itself" to a class "for itself".

After the revolution comes a phase of the dictatorship of the proletariat. Then the state withers away.

In the Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875), Marx describes two stages. In the first, each gets according to work. In higher communism: "From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs!"

• Economic determinism: Weber showed ideas, like the Protestant ethic, also shape the economy. Engels himself later said the economy is decisive only "in the last instance".
  • Prediction failed: revolution came in peasant Russia and China, not industrial Britain. Capitalism adapted through welfare and unions.
  • Karl Popper called historicism unfalsifiable.
  • Totalitarian outcomes in the USSR. Defenders reply that Stalinism betrayed Marx.
  • Yet the 2008 crash revived interest in his account of crises and inequality.

In articles for the New York Daily Tribune (1853), Marx said British rule in India had a "double mission": one destructive (breaking the old village society) and one regenerating (railways, a unified market). He wrote of an unchanging "Asiatic mode of production". Scholars now see this as Eurocentric.

Indian Marxists include M.N. Roy and E.M.S. Namboodiripad. Historians like D.D. Kosambi and Irfan Habib used Marxist methods.

Ambedkar criticised Indian communists for ignoring caste.

"Explain Marx's theory of alienation."
"Is Marxism relevant in the 21st century?"
"Discuss historical materialism and its critique."

Structure: three sources, base and superstructure (draw it), class struggle and modes of production, alienation, surplus value, revolution and communism. End with critique and relevance: inequality, the gig economy, platform capitalism.

quiz.q: Which work contains the famous base-superstructure passage?
o: 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy
quiz.w: The 1859 Preface gives the classic summary of historical materialism.

o: Value created by workers beyond their wage
quiz.w: Workers produce more value than they are paid; the surplus becomes profit.

quiz.q: 'From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs' appears in…
Which is NOT one of the forms of alienation in the 1844 Manuscripts?
quiz.w: The four are from product, labour, species-being and other people.

quiz.q: Marx's view that British rule in India had a destructive and a regenerating role is called…
quiz.w: From his 1853 articles in the New York Daily Tribune.
